transcript:
[00:00] Sofia Martinez (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we wanted to run through the POC SLO definition, get aligned on TTFT versus TPOT weighting and lay out a concrete load sweep and sampling plan. I think we have around an hour. Uh, quick intros?
[00:12] Lena Park (Aster): Hi, Lena here, engineering manager on the inference team. Our main thing is productionizing chat and a few batch embed jobs.
[00:20] Raj Patel (Aster): Raj, ML infra. We manage the model endpoints and cost allocation.
[00:26] Ethan Cole (Redwood SE): Ethan from Redwood, I'll be running the bench and walking through the measurement methodology.
[00:32] Ava Chen (Aster SRE): Ava, SRE, focused on latency budgets and alerting.
[00:38] Tom Rivers (Product): Tom from product, mostly here to confirm success criteria.
[00:44] Speaker 1: (mumble) yep
[01:05] Sofia: Cool. High level — we usually split latency SLO discussion into two complementary metrics: TTFT, time to first token, and TPOT, per-token throughput/latency (we sometimes call it per-token time). For conversational routes TTFT matters more for perceived snappiness, for long generation or streaming flows TPOT/p95 per-token is often the cost/throughput lever.
[01:25] Lena: Makes sense. For us, the chat widget is sensitive — product wants <450ms p95 TTFT for 8 tokens initial response under normal load. Under peak (burst) we can tolerate up to 700ms p95 but want to keep p99 under 1.2s.
[01:40] Ethan: Good to capture those numbers. One subtlety is that TTFT can be dominated by first-token compute or network setup and cold KV cache misses. We'll want to test both warm and cold cache states.
[01:55] Raj: On cache — can you spell that out? We have prefix caching in our current infra but not KV cache at model-level.
[02:03] Ethan: Sure — two things: prefix/KV cache at the runtime reduces repeated compute for similar prompts; a miss adds a small but measurable delta to TTFT. Also model quantization and batch shaping affect TPOT. We'll include permutations in the sweep.
[02:20] Ava: From reliability perspective we need p99s for both metrics. Even if product tolerates higher p99, we must know tail risk.
[02:30] Sofia: Agreed. We propose an acceptance matrix that weights metrics per route: chat route: 70% weight to TTFT p95, 20% to TPOT p95, 10% to p99 tail; batch embed route: 10% TTFT, 80% TPOT p95, 10% p99. That way final pass/fail is a weighted score. Thoughts?
[02:50] Tom: The weighted approach is reasonable as long as we can map to cost implications — if optimizing TTFT increases cost 30% that needs to be visible.
[03:02] Ethan: We'll output a cost vs latency curve. Our bench scripts capture GPU utilization, effective tokens/sec, and token cost estimate.
[03:15] Raj: For traffic profile, we'll send you a CSV with per-route QPS distribution and percent of long vs short responses.
[03:22] Sofia: Perfect. Now on measurement: recommended percentiles are p50, p95, p99 for both TTFT and per-token. For TPOT we'll measure tokens/sec per request and convert to per-token ms; note that for very short responses variance is high.
[03:38] Lena: Are you suggesting to treat very short responses differently?
[03:42] Ethan: Yes — we'll bucket requests by expected response length (short: <=16 tokens, medium: 17-128, long: >128) and compute metrics per bucket. That avoids skewing TPOT for tiny responses.
[03:55] Ava: Makes sense. We also need a sampling plan for quality checks — we don't want to run full human evals for every sweep.
[04:02] Sofia: Right. Proposed sampling: for each sweep point, sample 200 completions across representative prompts (stratified by bucket). We'll run automatic linting and a smaller human review set of 20 examples targeted at known risky prompts.
[04:18] Tom: That seems doable. How do you ensure the sampling covers distribution?
[04:22] Ethan: We'll weight by historical frequency from customer-provided profile and include a random seed for reproducibility. We'll also include a small adversarial subset from product.
[04:32] Raj: On load-sweep schedule — what's the plan? We want to understand both steady-state p95 and transient behavior under ramp.
[04:38] Sophia: (laughs) Sofia — load sweep plan is: start single-concurrency baseline, then ramp QPS in steps (25%, 50%, 75%, 100%, 150% of expected peak) holding at each step for 5 minutes for steady-state metrics and then run a 10-minute ramp test to observe queuing and latency curves. We'll repeat with KV caching enabled/disabled and with batching profiles changed (max batch size 8 vs 32).
[04:59] Ava: How do you capture warmup effects?
[05:01] Ethan: We recommend a 10-minute warmup at each config before capturing metrics. Also run a cold-start case: spin up instances from zero to simulate scale-up latency.
[05:12] Lena: Can you explain how TTFT vs TPOT tradeoffs show up during the sweep?
[05:16] Ethan: Sure — increasing batch size improves TPOT (tokens/sec) but often increases TTFT because requests wait to form batch. For conversational UX you may prioritize TTFT and accept lower TPOT; for batch you invert that. The weighted acceptance matrix ensures we can tune per-route.
[05:34] Tom: We have a question about percentiles — how do you ensure p99 is stable with limited sample sizes?
[05:40] Sofia: Good question. For p99 we need large samples; our sweep holds at least 5 minutes at target QPS which yields thousands of samples. We'll also do repeated runs and compute bootstrap confidence intervals.
[05:52] Raj: Any tooling we need to run on our side?
[05:55] Ethan: We'll provide a load harness (k6 script + wrapper) and a collector that emits detailed per-request JSON to S3 (or you can push to your data plane). We can run from Redwood hosted runner or within your VPC.
[06:08] Ava: Security checklist — we need SOC2, SSO/SAML, KMS integration. Will these be provided for the pilot?
[06:15] Sofia: Yes — we'll send SOC2 summary and our private deployment checklist. For pilot we can run on Redwood Hosted with encrypted transport; for Dedicated/Private we have options and can show KMS flow.
[06:24] Speaker 1: (inaudible)
[06:28] Ethan: A couple of gotchas from past pilots: 1) not isolating long-running batch jobs from chat traffic during sweep — we recommend separate routes with dedicated concurrency caps; 2) not toggling quantization consistently — always record model config.
[06:42] Lena: For success criteria — besides weighted score, product wants a go/no-go threshold: weighted score >= 85% and p99 delta vs baseline less than 2x.
[06:52] Sofia: We'll bake that into the acceptance matrix and show pass/fail per route.
[06:58] Tom: Timeline?
[07:00] Sofia: Proposed 4-week pilot: week 0 (this week) alignment and dataset handoff; week 1 baseline small sweep and iteration; week 2 full sweep and sampling; week 3 validation and pre-production runbook handover. We can compress if you commit to faster artifact delivery.
[07:16] Raj: That works. We can aim to provide prompts and profile by Friday (2026-12-05).
[07:22] Ava: Who owns the initial run? Redwood?
[07:25] Ethan: We'll run the initial baseline and share raw traces; then we'll hand over the harness for you to run within VPC if you prefer.
[07:33] Lena: On measurement artifacts, can you include GPU utilization and per-token cost estimate?
[07:38] Sofia: Yes, cost curves and GPU % utilization will be in the spreadsheet. We'll also annotate where caching or quantization changed config.
[07:45] Tom: Any blockers on our side?
[07:47] Raj: Security sign-off but that's normal. We need the SOC2 and KMS notes.
[07:52] Sofia: We'll attach that in the follow-up email.
[07:56] Ethan: Quick note on per-token measurement units — sometimes tracer reports tokens/sec which is inverted for intuitive latency (ms/token). We'll include both and a conversion column.
[08:10] Speaker 1: (crosstalk)
[08:15] Lena: I have one last question: for long-tail p99, how do you attribute to infra vs model variance?
[08:21] Ethan: We capture full request traces including model logits timing and runtime-side queuing. We'll run control experiments toggling model size/quantization to separate model compute from infra-induced queuing.
[08:33] Ava: Good. That separation is critical for our incident post-mortems.
[08:37] Sofia: OK, let's recap next steps and action items. Raj will share prompts and profile by 12/05. Sofia send benchmark template and security docs on 12/03. Ethan run baseline small-sweep and post logs by 12/06. Follow-up call Wednesday 2026-12-09 15:00 UTC.
[08:55] Tom: Fine by me. Thanks everyone.
[09:00] Sofia: Thanks, we'll follow up with the sheet and script links. Bye.
[09:03] (call ends)
